Reasons for Sentence of the
Honourable

A.A. Fradsham

Introduction

[
1
]

Mr. Mackenzie has pleaded guilty to two sets of charges, both arising
from incidents occurring on December 3, 2015.

[
2
]

The most serious charges are those arising from offending conduct
involving spray painting public property and private vehicles. That conduct led
to a charge of mischief and a charge of communicating statements in a public
place which were likely to lead to a breach of the peace by inciting hatred
against Syrians.  In summary, Mr. Mackenzie painted on public transit property
and parked private motor vehicles various statements calling for the killing or
bodily harm of Syrians. He thereby damaged the property upon which he painted,
and violated a provision of Canada’s criminal laws prohibiting what are
generally called “hate crimes”. The Crown proceeded by way of indictment.

[
3
]

The second set of charges involved a further act of mischief and
breaching the terms of a probation order. The Crown proceeded by way of summary
conviction procedure.

[
4
]

The current proceedings have as their task the determination of fit
sentences for Mr. Mackenzie’s offending conduct.

The Facts

The Offence (Information 160233375P1)

[
5
]

On December 3, 2015, Mr. Mackenzie spray-painted messages about Muslims
and Syrians on property owned by private individuals and the City of Calgary.
The offences took place at and around the Tuscany LRT station located in
Northwest Calgary at approximately 5:45 p.m. Mr. Mackenzie spray-painted while another
individual stood watch. Mr. Mackenzie spray-painted the following messages on
cars which were parked in the Tuscany LRT parking lot (spelling errors in the
messages are reproduced):

a)

Mistubishi
Outlander – a swastika on passenger rear door and “Kill Syrians” on front
passenger fender.

b)

Hyundai
Santa Fe – swastika on rear passenger side window and “Kill Syrans Fuck
Muslums” on front and back passenger side doors.

c)

Honda
Fit – “Kill Musilums” on passenger side windows and doors.

d)

Volkwagen
Jetta – swastika and “Kill Muslums Fuck ISIS” on right side of vehicle.

e)

Toyota
Yaris – “Fuck Syryia Kill Musilums” on passenger side doors and windows.

[
6
]

Mr. Mackenzie also spray-painted the following messages on the ramp of
the Tuscany LRT station and on the walls and exterior surfaces of the station –
“Fuck Musilums Fuck Syria” (ramp), “Fuck Musilim Goofs” (exterior door beside
entrance), “Fuck ISIS Musilum Fucks” (interior wall of station), “Fuck Syrian
Refs” (interior station window), “Fuck Syrea Kill Musilums” (inside staircase
exterior).

[
7
]

Mr. Mackenzie spray-painted the following messages on the interior of a
C-Train car – “Fuck ISIS Syran Refuges Not Welcome” (interior window and seat)
and “Fuck ISIS” (seat).

[
8
]

The monetary damage to the City of Calgary owned property is estimated
at $20,000. The monetary damage to the vehicles is not yet determined.

[
9
]

CCTV cameras photographed Mr. Mackenzie committing the offences. His
identity was confirmed by a Calgary Drop-in Centre employee who recognized him,
and by a police officer who compared a known photograph of Mr. Mackenzie to the
CCTV images. Mr. Mackenzie was arrested on December 9, 2015. In his interview
with the police, Mr. Mackenzie stated the following:

I did all of the tagging as I was mad at ISIS because they
shot up the people of Paris and I am a French Canadian. I don’t hate all
Muslims but I do hate what ISIS stands for. I am glad that it made the media as
I want to be famous for something and I wanted to come to jail for the winter.
The tagging was all my idea. Miguel Lavergne was with me but he did not do any
of the tagging.

The Offence (Information 151473410P1)

[
10
]

On December 3, 2015, at approximately 7:50 p.m., Mr. Mackenzie entered a
gas bar and threw down commercial displays causing $500 damage.  He threatened
one employee and assaulted another. He said that he wanted to go back to gaol,
and asked that the police be called.  He waited for the police to arrive.  Mr. Mackenzie
admitted that he had consumed “five beers”.  He was on a probation order which
required him to keep the peace and be of good behavior and to not consume
alcohol.

The Offender

[
11
]

At the time of these offences, Mr. Mackenzie was 28 years old. He has

[
12
]

I have had the benefit of both a Pre-Sentence Report (Exhibit 2)
prepared by a probation officer, and a Pre-Sentence Assessment (Exhibit 3)
prepared by Dr. Yuri Metelitsa who is a Psychiatrist, Forensic Psychiatry
Division of the Calgary Regional Department of Psychiatry, and a Clinical
Associate Professor in the Department of Psychiatry at the University of
Calgary.

[
13
]

I accept the statements of fact and opinions expressed by Dr. Metelitsa
in his report.

[
14
]

Mr. Mackenzie has a long history of substance abuse and mental health
difficulties. He was in a group home from ages 14 years to 18 years due to
behaviour problems  His early history was summarized by Dr. Metelitsa:

Mr. Mackenzie’s mother reported that her son began a lengthy
involvement with the psychiatric and child welfare systems at approximately age
12.  He was suspected of having Attention Deficit Disorder (ADD) as a child but
reported when placed on a trial of ADD medications, he responded with the
opposite reaction anticipated to the medications in that he appeared to be more
hyperactive.  She recalled her son had been placed in hospital on one occasion
but as he was screaming at the security staff, he was released to his parents.
Upon returning home, his behaviour escalated and he was found with a knife to
his throat.  He was subsequently returned to the Foothills Medical Center (FMC)
at which time he was assessed at the Young Adult Program.

Mr. Mackenzie’s mother reported that she and her husband
worked closely with their son’s various placements to provide consistency in
rules and expectations when he visited the home.  Given Mr. Mackenzie’s
continued disruptive behaviour and a need for structure and routine, Child
Welfare was able to extend his care through to age 21 at which time he was
transitioned to receiving supports through Persons with Developmental
Disabilities (PDD). Mr. Mackenzie’s mother advised her son has a public trustee
with respect to his finances and she continued to be her son’s legal guardian.

As an adult, Mr. Mackenzie has continued to require
supportive housing placements.  As per AHS records, Mr. Mackenzie has accessed
resources from a variety of providers including Canadian Mental Health
Association (Hamilton house), Vecova (Helios Program) and various placements
through Vantage Enterprises. As indicated in Dr. Xie’s report, Mr. Mackenzie
can no longer access housing through CMHA due to negative behaviours.  As per
Ms. Martin, Mr. Mackenzie was placed at the Helios Program through Vecova but
lost his placement there.  She advised Mr. Mackenzie accessed the support of
Vantage Enterprises 2.5 years ago after Ms. Mackenzie advocated for PDD
supports for Mr. Mackenzie.  Whilst engaged with Vantage, Mr. Mackenzie has
exhausted a multitude of supported roommate placements. As per Ms. Martin, Mr. Mackenzie
was initially placed in a home with considerable rules and structure.  She
reported he did well for six months although complained regularly about the
structure. He was subsequently placed in other supported roommate settings
though never with children given his history of altercations.  Ms. Martin
indicated Mr. Mackenzie was placed with a couple who were highly skilled but
the placement lasted three months. On February 28, 2009, Mr. Mackenzie was
evicted from his group home placement due to cocaine abuse. He was taken to
Renfrew Recovery by his father.  At Renfrew Recovery he was observed speaking
to a lamp, “Sid”, and saying “Sid” was commanding him to kill everyone at
Renfrew Recovery. At the hospital, he stated he was hearing voices but they
were much quieter.  He was evicted from Hamilton House in 2009 due to drinking
and then he lived at Helios House for 4 to 5 months until a placement with a
“supportive roommate” was arranged.  He was evicted from the Centre of Hope because
of possession of Xanex that he nought off the street (July 2009).

With respect to education, Mr. Mackenzie attended school at a
normal age. He had a history of academic difficulties. His mother reported that
her son attended a regular school placement until grade six and managed quite
well with average marks.  At age 12, Mr. Mackenzie’s negative behaviours
escalated and seemed to coincide with the transition to junior high school.
Mr. Mackenzie attended the William Roper School in Calgary for Grades 9-11 due
to behavioural difficulties.

[
15
]

Mr. Mackenzie has worked sporadically as a labourer, gas bar attendant,
stock person at a Canadian Tire store, garbage compactor, and worker at a pet
store. His longest stay in one position was one year (Canadian Tire).  He
required the “extensive support of a job coach” in order to keep a job.  He
currently receives Assured Income for the Severely Handicapped due to
Asperger’s Disorder.

[
16
]

Mr. Mackenzie first drank alcohol at the age of 8 years, but did not
drink again until he was 21 years old.  After recommencing alcohol consumption,
he drank as much as 16 cans of beer each weekend. He admits to having used
Cannabis, cocaine, mushrooms, LSD and crack cocaine. Though the details are not
clear about his current consumption (he denied use for the past four years but
that claim is false in light of the admissions  made in relation to the breach
of probation offence), it is clear that he has a significant polysubstance
dependency problem.

[
17
]

As for Mr. Mackenzie’s psychiatric history, Dr. Metelitsa said:

Mr. Mackenzie’s psychiatric history began when he was
approximately 12 years old.  In May 2000, he was seen at FMC. He attended the
Young Adult Program.  Psychological assessment revealed full IQ 89, verbal IQ
101 and performance IQ 79.  He was diagnosed with Generalized Anxiety Disorder
and ADHD.

Based on the available information, I understand that over
the years of his subsequent encounters with Mental Health Services, Mr. Mackenzie
has been diagnosed with Asperger’s disorder, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder,
PDD, oppositional defiant disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, alcohol
dependence, antisocial personality disorder, and polysubstance dependence.

Mr. Mackenzie has frequently accessed emergency departments
at various Calgary hospitals due to stressors such as housing issues or
physical altercations.  At times he indicated the presence of command
hallucinations (for example FMC discharge summary dated 2009 August 7).  The
diagnosis by Dr. Power on that occasion was Asperger’s and Antisocial Traits.

As indicated above, in November 2011 - January 2012 Mr. Mackenzie
underwent a forensic psychiatric assessment at SAFPC. At that time his
attention and concentration were good for short periods of time.  He then
starting cracking his knuckles loudly and fidgeting is his seat.  His affect
was blunted and did not fluctuate no matter the topic being discussed.  Mr. Mackenzie
acknowledged mood swings and anxiety attacks.  He described panic-like symptoms
(dizziness, feelings of unreality, butterflies in his stomach, and shaking) in
crowded places, shopping malls, planes, and jail because of a fear of having a
panic attack and dying. These symptoms could last several hours as long as he
is in the aversive situations.  He felt he had great social skills in the
community and was better able to function, which is not reflected in the file
information.  There was no evidence of hallucinations or paranoia.  Results of
the psychological assessment revealed an individual with intellectual abilities
in the high end of the Low Average range.  Mr. Mackenzie was diagnosed with
Alcohol Dependence, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, and Asperger’s Disorder.  He
also was diagnosed with Antisocial Personality Disorder.  His risk of
re-offending was rated as high.

According to AHS documentation, Mr. Mackenzie was released
following a six-month sentence and presented to Sheldon Chumir to request a
prescription for Clonazepam as he stated he felt anxious having not had his
pills. He was provided a one-week prescription for Olanzapine, Clonazepam, and
Citalopram.  He subsequently has been assessed and treated on many occasions in
the emergency departments when he was seeking admission to hospital, or when he
was brought by police due to his suicidal threats.

According to Psychiatric Emergency Services Consult Note, on
August 29, 2013, Mr. Mackenzie presented to the SHC, on a Form 10, after
calling police stating he wanted to jump from the bridge at Anderson LRT
station wanting to kill himself because he is a loser.  Mr. Mackenzie’s alcohol
level was documented by Clara Hlabangana to be 60 mmol at 22:00 hours; he was
assessed by the doctor at 08:00. He was diagnosed with toxic effects of alcohol
and housing issues, having become homeless two weeks prior, and was referred to
the Street Outreach Stabilization Program and the PORT team to meet the
following day.  Mr. Mackenzie reported to social worker, Nicole Mullen, he had
been diagnosed with schizophrenia and began receiving AISH at age 18.

As indicated above, in the end of 2013 - beginning of 2014,
Mr. Mackenzie underwent forensic psychiatric assessment at SAFPC.  At that time
he was fully orientated and did not display any psychotic symptoms.  He
followed the unit routine and participated in the unit activities.  While
talking about his history, including numerous incidents of violent behaviours
and multiple appearances at emergency departments, he demonstrated an obvious
tendency towards minimization, justification and attribution of his behaviour
to external events.  He also made a statement that some of his acts of physical
aggression are not random but rather directed towards individuals that are
“disrespectful” towards him.  He admitted that his alcohol use was a primary
factor in his aggressive and violent behaviours.  He did not show any signs of
remorse and, based on his previous experiences, appeared to be undeterred by
the criminal justice system.  Based on the results of the assessment the writer
diagnosed Mr. Mackenzie with Alcohol Dependence, as well as with Antisocial
Personality Disorder (combined with prominent traits of borderline personality
disorder).  It was noted a historical diagnosis of Asperger’s disorder.  Mr. Mackenzie’s
risk of re-offending was rated as very high.  The writer noted the striking
difference between Mr. Mackenzie’s unsettled behaviours in the community
(characterized by multiple appearances at the emergency departments) and his
completely settled behaviour during all his stay[s] at SAFPC, which is the good
evidence that he would [be] functioning much better in a controlled
environment.

I understand that following Mr. Mackenzie’s discharge from
SAFPC and subsequent release from custody, he continued to abuse alcohol and
street drugs, and has multiple presentations due to exacerbations of his mental
difficulties.

On May 14, 2014, the patient was referred to the Peter Lougheed
Centre (PLC) from CCC. Dr. Smith indicated the patient appeared to have issues
with alcohol dependence, polysubstance dependence, personality disorder NOS
(antisocial, borderline, dependent traits), and “may have Asperger’s disorder.”
The patient was subsequently returned to CCC.

As per the Foothills Medical Centre (FMC) September 8, 2014,
Consultation Note, Mr. Mackenzie was released from CCC on June 13, 2014, and
subsequently jumped off a bridge sustaining a number of injuries.  Dr. Terriff
indicated in his consultation, Mr. Mackenzie engaged in the aforementioned
behaviour as he, “did not feel accepted.” Mr. Mackenzie was an inpatient at the
FMC Unit 44 from June 13, 2014, to September 15, 2014; whereupon, he received
medical treatment for the injuries he incurred.  Dr. Terriff indicated in his
Consultation Note, dated September 8, 2014, Mr. Mackenzie sustained a number of
injuries of serious physical injuries and opined, “the prognosis for his
recovery of nerve injury will be slow and his long-term prognosis is guarded,
especially in the distal muscle where it could take up to 2 years to fully
recover.”

On September 20, 2014, Mr. Mackenzie presented to the
Emergency Department at Rockyview General Hospital (RGH) on a Form 10, after he
voiced suicidal ideation and disclosed he wanted to “jump off a bridge”.  In
the History and Physical Assessment, Dr. J. Chu noted the patient reported his
mood as a “6 out of 10” and his affect was euthymic, reactive and his mood
congruent. He indicated Mr. Mackenzie’s thought process was goal directed and
logical and he denied any obsessions or delusion; although, did indicate ideas
of thought insertion and broadcasting that were “not delusional intensity.” Dr.
Chu reported the patient described command type hallucinations that were
intermittent and “may have just been his own internal thought process and he
denied suicidal ideation or command hallucinations presented at the time.” Dr.
Chu diagnosed Mr. Mackenzie with: Polysubstance Use Disorder, Antisocial
Personality Disorder, and Autism Spectrum Disorder.

On September 26, 2014, Mr. Mackenzie was admitted to the
PLC.  Dr. R. Urquhart reported in his Discharge Summary, “on the short stay
unit, Mr. Mackenzie advised me of his ‘delusions’ and described some as: ‘I
still feel there’s some sort of weird conspiracy’ ‘delusional thoughts of
cameras are following me’ ‘I have weird delusions I’ve changed the world
somehow.’ Dr. Urquhart indicated that despite Mr. Mackenzie’s multiple
complaints of hallucinatory experiences, “there was no significant psychiatric
symptomatology.” Mr. Mackenzie was discharged with a referral to follow up with
the Forensic Assessment Outpatient Services (FAOS).

Mr. Mackenzie was admitted to the PLC short stay unit on
October 20, 2015, after being released from CCC and, “indicating he was
suicidal” after serving ten month sentence for assault with a weapon.  Whilst
an inpatient, Dr. T. Lo reported Mr. Mackenzie told him about the, “illuminati
conspiracy, and that others were stealing his ideas to profit from him, such as
family guy episodes.” Dr. Lo opined the patient displayed “no persecutory
themes, no paranoia on the unit, and the MSE did not indicate any impaired
sensorium and he did not report to internal stimuli.”  He further opined the
patient exhibited significant antisocial behaviours. Dr. Lo reported in his
Discharged Summary, planning for discharge involved the Corrections Transition
Team (CTT) who expressed concerns about future violence, especially if
intoxicated and with his expressed desire to return to jail.  As per the
Discharge Summary, Mr. Mackenzie would advise clinicians he was suicidal for
secondary gain; specifically, in jail, as “he voiced SI when he would like to
be in solitary confinement and have his own space away from others.” The
patient was transferred to Unit 27 on October 27, 2015, to coordinate a complex
case meeting with the involved agencies. Dr. Lo indicated “we were able to have
a meeting with CTT, his father Jim, we contacted his PDD worker, and CTT
collaborated with Regional Housing as well as his parole officer.”  The patient
was discharged on November 20, 2015.

[
18
]

On each of November 26, 2015, and December 1, 2015, Mr. Mackenzie
attended Calgary hospital emergency departments in relation to substance abuse.

[
19
]

Since December, 2014, Mr. Mackenzie has had the benefit of many
government assisted accommodation placements through Persons with Developmental
Disabilities (PDD), but each one has been terminated due to Mr. Mackenzie’s
behaviour.  As noted by Dr. Metelitsa reported:

With regard to eligibility for future
support with PDD, Ms. Sullivan advised Mr. Mackenzie is not actively in receipt
of any provincial funding for PDD supports at this time; however, he is still eligible
to access PDD services in the future if he displays a “change in behaviour.”
Ms. Sullivan opined, at the present time, Mr. Mackenzie puts [her] support
staff and others at risk; and all PDD agencies have said no to his referral.
Ms. Sullivan indicated that due to Mr. Mackenzie’s “substantial history of
violence,” addictions, mental health, and “potential inability to live with
others,” PDD has struggled with supporting him.

[
20
]

Dr. Metelitsa reported that during the time that Mr. Mackenzie was being
assessed for this current sentencing, Mr. Mackenzie “displayed little empathy
or regret for his behavior” in committing the offences.

[
21
]

Dr. Metelitsa came to the following conclusions:

Based on the results of the current
assessment, it is my opinion that Mr. Mackenzie’s mental difficulties can best
be categorized (according to DSM V criterial) as Alcohol and Polysubstance Use
Disorder (with possible past history of drug-induced psychotic episodes).  He
is also presenting as an individual with Antisocial Personality Disorder
(combined with prominent traits of borderline personality disorder).  In
addition, I cannot rule out (but cannot confirm) the diagnosis of Asperger’s
disorder.

It is my opinion that despite his mental
difficulties, Mr. Mackenzie is capable to appreciate (
sic
) the nature
and quality of his charges.  He is also able to follow court proceedings and to
advise [counsel].

With respect to the risk of re-offending it
should be indicated that Mr. Mackenzie is diagnosed with alcohol and
polysubstance use disorder and, based on my understanding, most of his criminal
actions have occurred in a context of alcohol intoxication.  He is
characterized as [an] individual with a very low stress tolerance coupled with
high impulsivity, inability to appropriately manage his anger and appropriately
deal with interpersonal conflict, as well as inability to handle rejection or
perceived slights.  He also has an established pattern of physical aggression.
In addition, he presents as being easily influenced by higher functioning
antisocial co-patients, and would be eager to follow their directions.  I
should note that Mr. Mackenzie presents as an antisocial individual who has
also established a pattern of abusing the mental health system.  Based on his
documents mental health history, he tends to magnify his complaints or
embellish psychotic symptoms.  He also appeared to be undeterred by the
criminal justice system. It is also noted that Mr. Mackenzie did not show any
signs of remorse with respect to his unlawful actions related to the index
offences.  As I indicated in my previous report, it should be also emphasized
the striking difference between Mr. Mackenzie’s unsettled behaviours in the
community (characterized by multiple appearance at the emergency departments)
and his completely settled behaviour during all his stay[s] at SAFPC, which is
the good evidence that he would [be] functioning much better in a controlled
environment.

Given the above-indicated considerations, it
is my opinion that at this point in time the risk of re-offending should be
rated as very high.

Given the nature of Mr. Mackenzie’s
difficulties, he should be provided with an opportunity for
psychiatric/psychological management and follow-up.  Whenever Mr. Mackenzie
remains in the community, his psychiatric/psychological management and
follow-up can be offered by FAOS or similar service.  He has indication for
substance abuse treatment in the community.  As indicated above, Mr. Mackenzie
requires placement in a strictly controlled environment. I would recommend that
the release plan include in addition to housing arrangement to establish a
24-hour support and supervision, as well as an ongoing addiction treatment.

Mr. Mackenzie’s prognosis at this point in
time must remain extremely guarded.

[
22
]

Mr. Mackenzie filed and read letters in the sentencing hearing. They
were to the effect that he has changed his views about the “Syrian and Muslim
community”, and that due to learning about Christianity he now “no longer
feel[s] a hate towards other races” and has “love for all of mankind”. In light
of Dr. Metelitsa’s objective and recent assessment of Mr. Mackenzie’s attitude
about his offending behaviour, I give little weight to Mr. Mackenzie’s
protestations of regret and redemption voiced in the courtroom.

[
23
]

No victim impact statements were filed in these matters.

Law and Analysis

Crown position

[
24
]

The Crown submitted that in relation to the mischief and hate crime
offences, the appropriate sentence is a global sentence of 18 months
incarceration (to be reduced appropriately for pre-sentence custody) followed
by probation for two to three years (including 300 hours of community service
hours).
[1]
The Crown also made an
undisputed restitution claim of $250 (an insurance deductible) on behalf of one
of the aggrieved vehicle owners. Finally, the Crown submitted that a
section
109(1)
(a)
Criminal Code

firearms prohibition order should be made in
respect of Mr. Mackenzie.

[
25
]

In relation to the mischief and breach of probation offence, the Crown
submitted that a global sentence of 3 months incarceration consecutive to the
sentences for the mischief and hate crime offences was appropriate.

Defence position

[
26
]

The defence submitted that the appropriate sentence for the hate crime
and mischief charges is equivalent to the time served up to June 15, 2016 (Mr. Mackenzie
has been in custody since December 4, 2015).  As noted, the restitution order
was not disputed, though the firearms prohibition was contested.

[
27
]

Defence counsel agreed that an additional, consecutive 3 months should
be imposed in relation to the mischief and breach of probation offences.

Court’s Analysis

[
28
]

The negative emotions engendered by the very nature of the hate crime
present the greatest difficulty in this sentencing. Consequently, I start my
analysis by respectfully adopting the comments of Justice Galligan in
R.
v. Lelas
(1990)
1990 CanLII 6836 (ON CA)
, 41 O.A.C. 73 (Ont. C.A.).
[2]

His Lordship said at paragraphs 34-35:

34
Repugnant as the respondent's opinions and
beliefs are, he cannot be punished for them. I think, therefore, that a court
must ensure that a sentence could not be taken as imposing punishment for
beliefs or opinions.

35
It is not easy to decide upon a sentence
which will express society's abhorrence of this kind of conduct and yet not
impose, or give the appearance of imposing, punishment for the respondent's
beliefs and opinions. Arriving at a fair balance between those two competing
principles, each of which has latent emotional impact, is a delicate exercise….

[
29
]

Indeed, Mr. Dhillon, in appearing for the Crown
in the case at bar, quite fairly and properly made the same point at the
beginning of his submissions.

[
30
]

The sentencing objectives in this matter are
deterrence, denunciation, and latterly, rehabilitation.

[
31
]

The aggravating factors are Mr. Mackenzie’s
related criminal record for mischief offences, and the fact that he was on
probation when he committed the mischief and hate crime offences. Normally,
section 718.2(a)(i) would make the hate aspect of the offending behaviour an
aggravating factor, but it is already part of one of the offences for which
sentence is being passed. An additional aggravating factor is the reference to
violence in the painted statements.

[
32
]

The mitigating factor is the offender’s guilty
plea. I accept that it is some expression of remorse.  However, as noted above
Mr. Mackenzie's further protestations of remorse and reformation should receive
little weight as they are a recent and significant departure from his attitudes
as exhibited while being assessed by Dr. Metelitsa.  Again, while Mr. Mackenzie
must not be punished for any personal views which he might hold, the facts do
not support the view that, apart from the guilty plea, there is any additional
evidence of remorse.

[
33
]

One of the submissions made by the defence was
that Mr. Mackenzie’s offending conduct did not make him “the worst possible
offender”, and that the maximum penalty (2 years’ imprisonment) should be reserved
for the worst possible offenders and circumstances.  Justice Parrett’s comment
at paragraph 3 of
R. v. Noble

2008 BCSC 216
was relied upon: “To
start with, the maximum penalty is generally considered to be reserved for the
worst possible offender and the worst possible circumstances....”

[
34
]

In my respectful view, the Supreme Court of Canada has firmly rejected
the argument that the maximum penalty should be reserved for the worst possible
offenders and the worst possible circumstances. Generally, language such as
“worst offender” or “worst offence” should be avoided when performing a
sentencing analysis. The Supreme Court of Canada noted in
R. v. Cheddesingh

2004 SCC 16 (CanLII)
, [2004] 1 S.C.R. 433 (at paragraph
1
), that:

…
t
erms such as "stark horror", "worst offence" and
"worst offender" add nothing to the analysis and should be avoided.
All relevant factors under the
Criminal Code
, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46,
must be considered. A maximum penalty of any kind will by its very nature be
imposed only rarely (see A. Manson,
The Law of Sentencing
(2001),
at p. 106) and is only appropriate if the offence is of sufficient gravity and
the offender displays sufficient blameworthiness. As is always the case with
sentencing, the inquiry must proceed on a case-by-case basis.

[
35
]

This was reiterated by the Supreme Court of Canada in
R. v.
L.M,

2008 SCC 31 (CanLII)
, [2008] 2 S.C.R. 163, at paragraphs
20-22
:

20
In
R.
v. Cheddesingh
, [2004] 1 S.C.R. 433,
2004 SCC 16
, the Court
acknowledged the exceptional nature of the maximum sentence, but firmly
rejected the argument that it must be reserved for the worst crimes committed
in the worst circumstances. Instead, all the relevant factors provided for in
the
Criminal Code
must be considered on a case-by-case basis,
and if the circumstances warrant imposing the maximum sentence, the judge must
impose it and must, in so doing, avoid drawing comparisons with hypothetical
cases.

... terms such as
"stark horror", "worst offence" and "worst
offender" add nothing to the analysis and should be avoided. All relevant
factors under the
Criminal Code
... must be considered. A
maximum penalty of any kind will by its very nature be imposed only rarely ...
and is only appropriate if the offence is of sufficient gravity and the
offender displays sufficient blameworthiness. As is always the case with
sentencing, the inquiry must proceed on a case-by-case basis. [para. 1]

21
Even where a maximum sentence is imposed,
therefore, regard must be had to the trial judge's discretion, the
individualized nature of sentencing and the normative principles set out by
Parliament in ss. 718, 718.1 and 718.2
Cr. C.
There is
still a place in criminal law for maximum sentences in appropriate
circumstances.

22
Thus, the maximum sentence cannot be
reserved for the abstract case of the worst crime committed in the worst
circumstances. The trial judge's decision will continue to be dictated by the
fundamental principle that a "sentence must be proportionate to the
gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender"
(s. 718.1
Cr. C.
).

[
36
]

Consequently, I respectfully decline to follow
“worst possible circumstances” line of reasoning, and will follow the
directions found in cases such as
R. v. Cheddesing
,
supra
,
and
R. v. L.M.
,
supra
.

[
37
]

While sentencing is not an exercise in finding
cases with similar facts
[3]
, section 718.2(b) does require
that “a sentence should be similar to sentences imposed on similar offenders
for similar offences committed in similar circumstances”. A review of similar
cases, and their applications of the applicable sentencing principles, may
provide some assistance in honouring section 718.2(b).

[
38
]

Section 319 creates two distinct offences in relation to the incitement
of hatred. Under subsection (1), an offence is committed if such hatred is
incited by communicating statements in a public place and such incitement is
likely to lead to a breach of the peace. Under subsection (2), an offence is
committed by wilfully promoting hatred against an identifiable group by
communicating statements, other than in private conversations. The element of
“wilfully” required under subsection 319(2) was defined in
Mugesera v.
Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)

2005 SCC 40 (CanLII)
, [2005] 2 S.C.R. 100
,

as follows at paragraph 104:

…the use of the word "wilfully" in subs. (2)
suggests that the offence is made out only if the accused had as a conscious
purpose the promotion of hatred against the identifiable group, or if he or she
foresaw that the promotion of hatred against that group was certain to result
and nevertheless communicated the statements. Although the causal connection
need not be proven, the speaker must desire that the message stir up hatred.

[
39
]

In comparing the two subsections of section 319, Martin J.A. in
R.
v.

Buzzanga
(1979)
1979 CanLII 1927 (ON CA)
, 49 C.C.C. (2d) 369 (Ont.Ct.), concluded that
the “guilty mind required by subsection (1) is “something less than intentional
promotion of hatred” in subsection (2). The stringent standard of
mens rea

under subsection 319(2) serves the purpose of “limiting the incursion of s.
319(2) into the realm of acceptable (though perhaps offensive and
controversial) expression”.

[
40
]

The distinction between these two subsections is important to note
because the majority of cases dealing with section 391 specifically address s.
319(2). Even so, the cases still provide guidance as to where the case at bar
fits in the spectrum of sentencing cases dealing with the overall offence of
incitement of hatred.

Mr. Zvonimir Lelas, who was a member of the Ku Klux Klan and described
himself as racist, together with a companion, spray painted anti-semitic
symbols and slogans on and near a synagogue, on a Hebrew school building, and
on an automobile. The crime involved spray painting synagogues with swastikas
and the following messages: “smash the ZOG”- ZOG being an acronym for Zionist
Occupational Government; an anti-semitic term. Mr. Lelas’ companion also
spray-painted “WP” (being an abbreviation for “white power”) on the sides of
the synagogues. Mr. Lelas also spray-painted the following message on the
Hebrew school: “Nazism” and a swastika on the school sign, and the words “The
Wind is blown” with a Celtic cross beside it and “Zog has died” on the door of
the school. Finally, Mr. Lelas spray-painted a swastika on the hood of an
automobile. Mr. Lelas pleaded guilty to three charges of mischief to property
over $1,000. At trial, Mr. Lelas was sentenced to six months imprisonment
and two years’ probation. The Crown appealed that sentence imposed by the
Ontario Court of Justice. Justice Houlden allowed the appeal and increased Mr.
Lelas’ sentence to 1 year imprisonment and affirmed the probation order.
Houlden, J.A. justified this increase of imprisonment at paragraph 30:

In spray painting the synagogue and Hebrew school, Lelas was
not merely intending to cause damage to property; rather, to use his words, he
wanted "to enrage the Jewish community". His acts were done to strike
fear and terror and to cause emotional upset in the Jewish community. When
mischief is racially or religiously motivated and is done to cause emotional
injury or shock to a particular segment of Canadian society, it calls for a far
more severe penalty than mischief which is done merely to damage property.

[
42
]

In the judgment, Houlden, J.A. further stated that:

A sentence of six months is not, in my opinion, sufficient to
meet the needs of general deterrence and to show society's abhorrence of the
acts of the respondent. If it were not for the fact that Lelas has been
released and must be re- incarcerated, I would have imposed a longer sentence.
The message must go out loud and clear that conduct such as that engaged in by
the respondent will not be tolerated in Canadian society, and if it is engaged
in, it will be met with a severe penalty.

[
43
]

As I have already noted, in his dissent, Galligan J.A. agreed with
Houlden, J.A. about the gravity of the offences and about the reprehensibleness
of the accused’s conduct. However, Galligan, J.A. disagreed with the sentence,
noting that as “repugnant as the [accused’s] opinions and beliefs are, he
cannot be punished for them.  I think, therefore, that a court must ensure
that a sentence could not be taken as imposing punishment for beliefs or
opinions.” Galligan, J.A. discussed the intricate balance of deciding a
sentence which will both express society’s abhorrence of this kind of conduct
and “yet not impose, or give the appearance of imposing, punishment for the
[accused’s] beliefs and opinions.” Galligan, J.A. concluded that the sentence
of six months imposed by the trial judge provided a fair balance.

The Case at Bar

[
54
]

Mr. Mackenzie may have Asperger’s disorder, and
he does suffer from alcohol and polysubstance use disorder. He also has
antisocial personality disorder with prominent traits of borderline personality
disorder. As noted in Clayton Ruby’s book
Sentencing
,
7th
edition
(LexisNexis Canada Inc.; Markham, Ontario; 2008) at p. 298:

It is clear, therefore, that a sentence can be reduced on
psychiatric grounds in two instances: (1) when the mental illness has
contributed to or caused the commission of the offence; or (2) when the effect
of imprisonment or any other penalty would be disproportionately severe because
of the offender’s mental illness….

[
55
]

Neither ground applies to the case at bar.

[
56
]

Apart from Mr. Mackenzie making the general comment that “his alcohol
and substance abuse were important factors in his unlawful actions” (see
Exhibit 3 at p. 8), there is no evidence that the current offences were the
result of alcohol or drug ingestion.  In any event, in these circumstances I
would not consider any voluntary intoxication on his part to be a mitigating
factor.

[
57
]

I do not find Mr. Mackenzie’s described difficulties to be a true mitigating
factor.  They are relevant to this sentencing in that they inform the process
of crafting the rehabilitative aspects of the appropriate sentence.

[
58
]

Section 718.1 states that “a sentence must be proportionate to the
gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender”.  In
relation to the racial comments Mr. Mackenzie painted on the public property
and the privately owned motor vehicles, his conduct was highly offensive and
hurtful.  However, it was also primarily immature and juvenile.  The manner in
which Mr. Mackenzie generally conducts himself with other members of the
public, be they members of the public at large or those assigned the task of
trying to assist him, makes him, by any objective measure, a difficult and
unpleasant person with whom to interact.  For evidence supporting that
statement one has to look no further than Mr. Mackenzie’s “bridge burning” with
the agencies valiantly trying to find him stable housing.  Mr. Mackenzie is
simply an unpleasant fellow and it would appear that to date he is content to
be so.  As for his protestations of reformation made on the eve of this
sentencing, I find them to be, at best, reflective of future intention. His
past behaviour strongly suggests that they may be simply manipulative and
convenient.  His future conduct, after this sentencing, will help answer that
question.

[
59
]

However, what must be kept in mind is that Mr. Mackenzie’s offending
behaviour (in relation to the section 319(1) offence) was much less
ideologically motivated than it was an instance of “acting out” similar to that
which one often sees in unruly adolescents.  Mr. Mackenzie was thoughtless and
consequently hurtful in what he did, and indeed he made reference to violence in
his painted outbursts, but his acts were not the vicious, and evil acts of, for
example, the offenders in
R. v. Mahr
,
supra
, and
R.
v. Noble
,
supra
.  In my view, Mr. Mackenzie, while very, very
wrong in his actions, and deserving of meaningful punishment, is less morally
blameworthy (in relation to the section 319(1) offence) than either of Mr. Mahr
or Mr. Noble.

[
60
]

With respect, I am of the opinion that the period of incarceration
sought by the Crown in relation to the section 319(1) offence is not supported
by the sentencing precedents, nor is it proportionate to the gravity of the
particular offending behaviour, or to Mr. Mackenzie’s moral blameworthiness in
committing that offending behaviour. I am also of the view that it is
unrealistic to expect that Mr. Mackenzie would successfully complete community
service hours.

[
61
]

Finally, I note that I am particularly mindful of
section 718.2
(c) of
the
Criminal Code

which states that “where consecutive sentences are
imposed, the combined sentences should not be unduly long or harsh”.

Section 109(1)(a)

[
62
]

The Crown submitted that an order under
section 109(1)
(a) would be
appropriate. A question arose as to whether such an order could be lawfully
made in relation to the mischief charge on Information 160233375P1.  I am of

(a) applies.

[

]

Section 109(1)(a) stipulates that:

109

(1)
Where a person is convicted,
or discharged under section 730, of

(a)
an indictable offence in the commission of which
violence against a person was used, threatened or attempted and for which the
person may be sentenced to imprisonment for ten years or more,

the court that sentences the person or directs that the
person be discharged, as the case may be, shall, in addition to any other
punishment that may be imposed for that offence or any other condition
prescribed in the order of discharge, make an order prohibiting the person from
possessing any firearm, cross-bow, prohibited weapon, restricted weapon,
prohibited device, ammunition, prohibited ammunition and explosive substance
during the period specified in the order as determined in accordance with
subsection (2) or (3), as the case may be.

[
64
]

Section 109(1)(a) does not direct that a firearm prohibition is
mandatory upon conviction on a charge of mischief under section 430(3). Rather,
it directs that the prohibition is mandatory where violence is used, threatened
or attempted against “a person.” In my view, Mr. Mackenzie did, by the content
of the messages painted on the property, threaten violence to a person, notably
any person who is a Muslim, Syrian, or Syrian refugee. As such, a mandatory
firearms/weapons prohibition remains an available order which can be included as
part of a mischief charge under section 430(3).

Justice Côté said In

2011 ABCA 105
at
paragraph
7
:  “...In theory, trying to set some outer limits for a sentence
range by examining precedents has some utility, but in practice it is often
unsatisfactory. Typically the outer limits are too far apart to be meaningful,
and the facts are all over the map. Few if any cases really match on their
facts; so all one can ordinarily produce is a Frankenstein’s monster, by trying
to graft two or more precedents together. Use of precedent for factual
questions, especially for numbers for sentences or damages, is not usually a
useful exercise: R. v. Arcand,
2010 ABCA 363
(para.
216
) and R. v. Hennessey,

2010 ABCA 274
, 260 C.C.C. (3d) 499 (para.
80

1980 ABCA 227 (CanLII)
, 24 A.R. 181 (C.A.) (para.
20
). Instead,
the value of sentencing precedent lies in its principles and (where given) its
starting points.”
